# DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017

Technical Report 👁️

## Introduction **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017** is a minor update to [**DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash**](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), delivering substantial improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic tasks, and visual benchmarks. Alongside these gains, the model reduces task execution time and output length, enabling users to complete tasks faster and at lower cost and advancing the performance–cost Pareto frontier across multiple agent harnesses.
| Benchmark | DS-V4.1-Flash-1017 | DS-V4.1-Flash | K3 | GLM-5.3 | GPT-5.6 Sol | Opus 5 | | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | HLE w/o tools | 42.6 (44.0†) | 36.8 (39.1†) | 43.5 | 42.0† | 44.5 | 56.3 | | Terminal-Bench 4.0 | 42.3 | 31.2 | 12.6 | 37.9 | 39.9 | 51.8 | | DeepSWE v1.1 | 77.0 | 74.2 | 67.5 | 66.9 | 73.0 | 74.0 | | ProgramBench | 29.1 | 20.3 | 17.5 | 19.0 | 23.0 | 37.0 | | NL2Repo-Bench | 68.2 | 65.4 | 58.0 | 58.0 | 56.8 | 75.3 | | Automation-Bench v1.0.6 | 60.5 | 54.8 | 46.7 | 48.8 | 45.8 | 50.3 | | Agents’ Last Exam | 35.4 | 31.8 | 27.6 | 28.5 | 26.7 | 28.6 | | Apex Bench v1.1 | 72.1 | 64.6 | 47.8 | 56.6 | 54.3 | 65.8 | | Chartography (w/tools) | 83.0 | 78.9 | 68.1 | — | 79.9 | 84.0 | | BabyVision (w/tools) | 92.5 | 89.6 | 85.7 | — | 88.9 | 94.1 | | ZeroBench-main (w/tools) | 51.0 | 49.0 | 41.0 | — | 53.0 | 52.0 |
*† denotes the text-only subset of HLE. We use the Claude Code harness for Terminal-Bench 4.0 and the Mini-SWE-V2 harness for DeepSWE v1.1.* ## Prompt Encoding This release does not include a Jinja-format chat template. The [`encoding`](encoding/README.md) folder contains a self-contained Python reference implementation (`encoding.py`) with test cases for multi-turn conversations, tool calling, thinking mode, numeric reasoning effort, mid-conversation system messages, and interleaved image content. For production use, we additionally release [deepseek-recipe](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-recipe), a set of Rust libraries with Python bindings that provides the same prompt format as a maintained, protocol-aware toolkit. It converts Messages, Chat Completions, and Responses API requests into the Conversation format, encodes them into DeepSeek V4 and V4.1 prompts or token IDs, and parses model output back into complete or streamed responses — covering thinking, tool calls, images, and generation settings. Model inference, tool execution, and HTTP transport are left to the caller. ## Minimal Inference Please refer to the [`inference`](inference/README.md) folder for instructions on weight conversion and running inference locally. **Recommended sampling parameters:** | Parameter | Value | | :--- | :--- | | `temperature` | 1.0 | | `top_p` | 1.0 | | `context_window` | 1M tokens | | `max_tokens` | ≥ 256K | ## License This repository and the model weights are licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE). ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{deepseekai2026deepseekv41flash, title={DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression}, author={DeepSeek-AI}, year={2026}, } ``` ## Contact If you have any questions, please raise an issue or contact us at [service@deepseek.com](mailto:service@deepseek.com).

# MOSS-Image-SFT

                         

User guide   ·   中文用户指南   ·   ComfyUI

![MOSS-Image-Base and MOSS-Image-SFT](assets/teaser.webp) MOSS-Image-SFT is a supervised fine-tuned text-to-image model in the **MOSS-Image** family from OpenMOSS, derived from [MOSS-Image-Base](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Image-Base). It uses the same architecture and inference pipeline, supporting natural-language prompts, tag sequences, and JSON layouts for controlling text placement and object arrangement. ## Base vs. SFT In this example, SFT produces clearer text grouping and a more organized whiteboard layout. | MOSS-Image-Base | MOSS-Image-SFT | | --- | --- | | ![MOSS-Image-Base](assets/comparison/base.webp) | ![MOSS-Image-SFT](assets/comparison/sft.webp) | ## Quick start Use Python 3.10 or later and an NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support. Install a PyTorch 2.9 or later build compatible with your CUDA environment, then install: ```bash pip install "diffusers>=0.38" "transformers>=5.3" "accelerate>=1.10" "safetensors>=0.6" "Pillow>=10" ``` ```python import torch from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained( "OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Image-SFT", custom_pipeline="pipeline_moss_image", trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype={"default": torch.bfloat16, "vae": torch.float32}, ) pipe.scheduler = type(pipe.scheduler).from_config(pipe.scheduler.config) pipe.to("cuda") prompt = '''A wide view of a refrigerator beside a kitchen counter with a fruit bowl. A small sticky note on the refrigerator door is handwritten in Chinese: "记得买牛奶和鸡蛋！ 牛奶两盒，鸡蛋一打。 顺便带一袋面包。"''' image = pipe( prompt, height=1024, width=1024, num_inference_steps=50, guidance_scale=3.0, uncond_skip_layers=[22], generator=torch.Generator("cpu").manual_seed(42), ).images[0] image.save("refrigerator_note.png") ``` The model and custom pipeline code are downloaded and cached automatically. You can also pass a complete local model directory to `from_pretrained`. The transformer and text encoder use bfloat16; the VAE and initial noise use float32. The bundled VAE uses the FLUX.2 small decoder. For the Gradio interface, CPU offload, and compilation options, follow the [project quick start](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Image#quick-start). For ComfyUI, search for **MOSS-Image** in **ComfyUI Manager** to install the native plugin. Integration into the official ComfyUI repository is in progress. See the [installation and usage guide](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Image/blob/main/comfyui/README.md) and [example workflow](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Image/blob/main/comfyui/moss-image/example_workflows/moss-image.json). ## Sampling settings | Setting | Default | | --- | --- | | Sampler | Flow-matching Euler | | Steps | 50 | | CFG | 3 | | Shift | 5 | | Layer skipping | Negative branch, layer index 22 (zero-based) | | Negative prompt | Empty | The default guidance uses two transformer forwards per step. Pass `uncond_skip_layers=[]` to disable negative-branch skipping, or set `negative_prompt` to provide a negative prompt. Python API image dimensions must be positive multiples of 16. See the [user guide](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Image/blob/main/USERGUIDE.md) for resolution, sampling, prompt, and LoRA training recommendations. ## Prompt enhancer skill The [MOSS-Image Prompt Enhancer](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Image/blob/main/skills/moss-image-prompt-enhancer/SKILL.md) turns image ideas into detailed captions or spatial Layout prompts. It is designed for GPT-6-family agents with local file and Python tools. The bundled script converts pixel-coordinate drafts into compact JSON with integer centered coordinates; it does not call an image-generation service. Install the [skill folder](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Image/tree/main/skills/moss-image-prompt-enhancer) in your agent's skills directory, then invoke `$moss-image-prompt-enhancer` with your image idea, desired caption or Layout output, and any canvas dimensions. Paste the compiled result into MOSS-Image's positive prompt; for Layout, use the same generation dimensions. ## Layout-to-image generation Pass a JSON layout as the prompt to describe the scene, rendered text, objects, and their positions. Layouts use `summary.caption` and `items`, with `bbox_format: "yxyx"` and `bbox_coord_space: "abs_centralized"`. With the Python API, serialize the layout using `json.dumps(layout, ensure_ascii=False)` and pass it to `pipe`. In Gradio, paste the JSON into the Prompt field and set the matching image dimensions. See the [layout format and example](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Image/blob/main/USERGUIDE.md#layout-prompts-experimental). Layouts can also support controlled editing and user-friendly layout tools. Edit text, element descriptions, and bounding boxes to adjust image content and composition in a structured way. ![Layout control](assets/showcase/layout-bboxes.webp) ## Showcase ![Examples overview](assets/showcase/overview.webp) ![Examples overview 2](assets/showcase/overview2.webp) ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{ai2026mossimagetechnicalreport, title={MOSS-Image Technical Report}, author={MOSI. AI}, year={2026}, eprint={2610.23374}, archivePrefix={arXiv}, primaryClass={cs.CV}, url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23374}, } ``` ## License and acknowledgements The model weights and bundled inference code are released under the [Apache License, Version 2.0](LICENSE). We thank the Diffusers, Qwen, and FLUX teams.

tools.headline: OpenAI CLI: call OpenAI from your terminal to make images and manage files
tools.summary: Generate an image, upload a file, or submit a batch job straight from the command line, with no app code needed.
tools.why_it_matters: You can test OpenAI API calls or script them without writing an application, and it only needs an API key to start.
tools.for_builders: Run brew install openai/tools/openai, then openai help setup to add your API key.

extra.source_text: OpenAI CLI The official command-line tool for the OpenAI REST API. Install · CLI reference · Guides Call the OpenAI REST API from your terminal or shell scripts. Generate images, upload files, submit batches, and inspect API results without writing an application. Note OpenAI CLI or Codex CLI? Use openai when you want to call a specific API or put API operations in a script. Use Codex CLI ( codex ) when you want a coding agent to work on a project: read and edit code, run commands, and help implement or debug a change. Things to try These examples use an API key; see installation and authentication below. Generate an image and save it locally openai images generate --prompt " A tiny orange robot watering a houseplant " Images are saved to ~/Downloads/gpt-images/ , and the command prints their paths. Use --output-dir for an existing destination directory or --name for a filename. Supported terminals can preview the result. See the image guide for editing, model selection, and preview settings. Upload a file and retrieve it later openai files upload report.txt --purpose user_data openai files get file-example openai files download file-example --output downloaded-report.txt Use your own local file and replace file-example with the ID returned by the upload. See working with files for more examples. Run requests in a batch Submit a JSONL request file, then wait for the batch and download its results: openai files upload requests.jsonl --purpose batch openai batches create --input-file-id file-example \ --endpoint /v1/responses --completion-window 24h openai batches wait batch_example --output-dir ./results Replace the file and batch IDs with the returned IDs. The batch guide includes a sample requests.jsonl and explains result files and failed requests. Export API data for a script openai models list --format jsonl | jq ' .id ' openai files list --format json > files.json Choose --format json for a JSON document or --format jsonl for records. The default output is readable text, even in pipes . The first example uses jq . Installation Installing a prebuilt binary Download the archive for your operating system and architecture from GitHub Releases . Binaries are available for macOS, Linux, and Windows. Extract the archive and place openai ( openai.exe on Windows) in a directory on your PATH . Installing with Homebrew brew install openai/tools/openai Installing with Go Requires Go 1.26 or later . go install ' github.com/openai/openai-cli/cmd/openai@latest ' Once you have run go install , the binary is placed in your Go bin directory: Default location : $HOME/go/bin (or $GOPATH/bin if GOPATH is set) Check your path : Run go env GOPATH to see the base directory If commands aren't found after installation, add the Go bin directory to your PATH: # Add to your shell profile (.zshrc, .bashrc, etc.) export PATH= " $PATH : $( go env GOPATH ) /bin " Supported self-managed release installations prepare automatic updates during eligible interactive runs. Package-manager and Go installations retain update notices and their existing installation ownership. Set OPENAI_CLI_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1 to disable automatic installation, or OPENAI_CLI_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to disable all update checks. See automatic updates for installation requirements, exact-version pins, and activation behavior. Authentication Run the setup guide to enter your API key safely: openai help setup For scripts, supply OPENAI_API_KEY through your environment or secret manager. Create a key in API settings . Try a request: openai responses create \ --model gpt-5.5 \ --input " Say this is a test " Admin endpoints use OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY , a separate admin API key . For example, retrieve one day of organization usage: openai admin organization usage completions \ --start-time 1735689600 \ --end-time 1735776000 \ --bucket-width 1d Usage Commands follow the API's resources: openai < resource > [subresource...] < command > [flags...] Browse commands and options with help. Help needs no API key or network connection. openai --help openai images generate --help openai admin organization --help openai help COMMAND and openai COMMAND --help show the same page. Existing colon-separated commands, such as openai admin:organization:usage completions , also work. Output and errors Successful JSON responses display readable text by default. Select a data format explicitly when parsing results. Use --transform to extract fields with GJSON syntax : openai files get file-example --transform filename --raw-output Errors go to stderr as readable summaries. Use --format-error json for API error details, or --transform-error to extract error fields. Explicit --format json , jsonl , raw , and yaml also apply to errors unless --format-error overrides them; --format-error text restores summaries. API error details and --debug logs can contain sensitive data: sanitize them before sharing. --debug adds per-attempt HTTP timing. Add --debug-body for redacted JSON previews or --debug-sse --debug-event-timing for bounded stream diagnostics. See HTTP debugging for capture limits and timing boundaries. Check the command's exit status before using redirected results; a failed request can leave an incomplete output file. See reading command results for list formats, streaming, binary downloads, and error behavior. File input Binary uploads take a plain path. JSON input flags can read a value from a local file with @path : openai files upload report.txt --purpose user_data openai responses create --model gpt-5.5 --input @prompt.txt Use OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN=1 when piping JSON or YAML from an untrusted source so input cannot cause local file reads. In that mode, provide upload paths explicitly as flags. See file arguments and encoding for escaping literal @ values, JSON/YAML input, and text or base64 encoding. Shell shortcuts Set up shell completion to complete commands and file paths. Command insertion lets you search examples with Ctrl+X, then Tab and insert them without running them. ## 🎬 Feature presentation: OPUSCAR 98

▶ The film · 1927 – 2025 · 6:31
One Clawd walks through all 98 Best Picture winners, each one redrawn in a style that fits the film.
All 98 styles, open · 77 in 2D · 4 in 2.5D · 17 in 3D

[**▶ Watch**](https://lemomo-ai.github.io/lemo-opuscar/opuscar98/) · [**All 98 styles**](https://lemomo-ai.github.io/lemo-opuscar/opuscar98/#styles) · [**Download 1080p**](https://github.com/lemomo-ai/lemo-opuscar/releases/download/films/opuscar98.mp4)
## 👋 About me I'm **Lemomo** ([@lemomo-ai](https://github.com/lemomo-ai)). More about me on my profile. > **Not an awesome list.** Every film here was made by me, with Claude Opus 5.5.
> The styles are tuned for Opus 5.5; other models may not reproduce them. ![All styles](docs/cover.jpg) Every film was directed, drawn, scored and mixed by an AI agent writing code: - 🎨 **Picture**: canvas and WebGL pages, rendered frame by frame - 🎵 **Music**: original scores from free sample libraries - 🎙️ **Voice**: text-to-speech narration No video generation, no stock footage. ## How to use Two ways in; the skill is the easiest. ### Option 1: install the skill (recommended) In your terminal: ```sh claude plugin marketplace add lemomo-ai/lemo-opuscar claude plugin install lemo-opuscar@lemolab ``` Then use it from any folder. - On first use it downloads the guides, tools and style prompts to `~/lemo-opuscar`, shared by all your films. - Each film's project, from source to finished video, goes in the folder you started from. - For other agents, copy [`plugin/skills/lemo-opuscar/`](plugin/skills/lemo-opuscar/) into their skills folder. ### Option 2: clone the repo ```sh git clone https://github.com/lemomo-ai/lemo-opuscar.git cd lemo-opuscar claude ``` Films go into `films//` inside the repo. ### Then just say what you want > Make a 45-second film in the **watercolor** style about the coffee farm my family runs. Warm female narrator. > Make a 40-second **LiDAR Survey** film about the old quarry in the hills behind our town, from public laser-scan data. Name the style in English or Chinese; the [style index](styles/README.md) lists them all. Not sure yet? With the skill installed, type `/lemo-opuscar:lemo-opuscar` and nothing else. It asks which language to use, then what you'd like to do: a film in a library style, [make a style your own](#make-a-style-your-own), or a film in a style you've saved. It asks you once, up front: - anything it can't decide about your topic; - whether you have your own **voice, music or other material**; - whether you want to see a **storyboard** first. Say yes and it stops once to show you the key shots in the real style; otherwise it goes straight to the finished film. The agent reads three guides and works like a small studio: | File | What it gives the agent | |---|---| | [`DIRECTOR.md`](DIRECTOR.md) | how to direct: story, sound, rhythm, camera, performance, self-checks | | [`TECHNIQUE.md`](TECHNIQUE.md) | how to build: frame-by-frame rendering, voice, music, mixing | | `styles/

quick.headline: Ask HN: How do you ship AI-written code you don't fully understand?
quick.summary: Engineers on Hacker News share how they keep control, often by designing the structure themselves first.
quick.why_it_matters: If an AI writes most of your app, these habits help you know what the code does before it goes live.
quick.for_builders: Start small: agree on the structure with the AI in a short chat first, then have it implement one piece at a time.

extra.candidate_title: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
extra.source_text: Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand? 620 points by rzk 6 days ago | hide | past | favorite | 761 comments I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m... > I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I'm used to understanding what I'm building. Now I'm trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I'm comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too? How are you handling this? bitwizeshift 6 days ago | next [–] I’m surprised I haven’t see anyone say this yet, but I don’t let the LLM design the code at all, I let it implement a design I have created. By that I mean that, rather than let the LLM do the entire structure, I take the time to create the full hierarchy of abstractions and actors that I want my code to do. I decide, at the UML level, how abstractions will sit and interact — and then I make the LLM implement those gaps. The key thing here is that, by doing this, I DO know how the code works. I may not know how each unit is implemented, but I know each unit’s responsibilities and how they interact with one another. I’ve found that LLMs are HORRIBLE at writing decent abstractions, regardless of how much prompting and skills I’ve given it. It will always get the job done, but it will often be unmaintainable and require bigger and heavier refactors as I introduce more and more requirement changes. But by flexing my basic design skills, I don’t have those issues. Future refactoring fit into easy abstractions that I’ve designed. And by documenting it up front, I also have what becomes a living document on how this work will turn out. It takes a few hours up front to plan ahead, but it makes the LLMs job easier and use less tokens, and it makes the code better long term. I don’t care if one unit is suboptimal, as long as the abstraction is right — because at worst I can change an implementation for a better one later. reply davepeck 5 days ago | parent | next [–] A friend of mine sometimes jokes that code is “fractally busted” when it’s wrong at every level, from single lines all the way up to the design of the system’s main interfaces. That’s also roughly what I find after a long English-only session with a coding agent. Our conversation covers a lot of ground... and leaves out details at every level. When I look at what got built, the misunderstandings are fractal too. I agree it’s important to design it yourself, but UML is only one level. Lately I’ve been using a scratch Python file (or even a scratch repo) that Claude and I both edit. Never mind that I’m writing Rust. Python reads like pseudocode, and pass and ... (Ellipsis) let me skip whatever I don’t care about. At any level where I do care, I can say exactly what a method’s signature should look like, what fields a domain model should have, or how it should maintain key invariants. Everywhere else I leave an ellipsis, maybe a docstring, and let the agent decide. It works both ways: I ask the agent to sketch the current system in Python, with some details elided and others spelled out. Then I edit the sketch and have the agent push the changes back into the much bigger Rust+Tauri app. Time will tell whether this approach has legs, but when I want to be precise, I find it sometimes pays to just write some code. reply throwaway219450 5 days ago | root | parent | next [–] This is the way. I can write pseudo code (ie Python) and I leave a breadcrumb trail of comments where I want it to implement. Hell the code doesn’t even need to have valid syntax if you forgot some function signature, but that small amount of guiding can produce significantly better results than a blind implementation from the model. I’ve also tried spending an hour or two first before handing over control. That way there’s something pre-existing it can work from. reply stickfigure 5 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I don't have this experience at all. My workflow is: * Bite sized jobs, about what you would expect for a traditional user story. * 10-15 minutes discussing the implementation. It's almost the exact same conversation I would have with a human engineer. I'm almost entirely asking questions - "How would you do Xyz? What about this problem? What about that problem?" * At the end of the conversation, both the AI and I have a good understanding of the problem and the solution. * I say "do it". * There are occasions when I don't fully understand what it wants to do. I'll tell it to do the work, then we discuss it afterwards. Sometimes we change things, sometimes I just need to see the code to understand. * It doesn't commit code. I do. This has been really effective for me, easily 10X'd or more my pace of development. Sometimes I have to ask for a lot of rework and sometimes it one-shots it. But I never ship something I don't understand and it always feels like "my" code. Very satisfying. More satisfying than typing it all out; the typing was never the fun part of programming. reply zahlman 5 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I've found that current models will almost automatically sketch out some things in Python (or another suitable language for the type of task, or an implementation language you've already stipulated) while proposing a design, and you can go through a conversation of "what if we did xyz instead?" and at some point "okay, let's try writing a full prototype" (perhaps tacking on a bunch of decisions here so that things are resolved enough to work with). But that's at the scale of <1kloc. Might be different if you're trying to do a bigger feature all at once. reply jasonjayr 5 days ago | root | parent | next [–] I suspect that's a problem both with human read/written code, and LLM written code -- larger features should be chunked up into more manageable to understand and reason about functions, and assembled at higher levels. Guiding the LLM (or humans structuring/guiding juniors) to shape the abstractions help make the overall feature and reliability of the code much better. reply Shorel 5 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] There's something to your approach. The best results for me have been when I write something 100% in a language and when it is done the AI takes my implementation and ports it to another language. reply fasterik 6 days ago | parent | prev | next [–] I agree with this approach, but I'm a bit surprised this has to be said at all. These are basic software design principles and I imagine it's the default way any experienced programmer would approach the problem. I wonder if the people not using this approach are primarily junior developers who have never seen how real software is built, or if it's leaking into the senior levels as well. reply swatcoder 6 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Most people in the industry right now, even at FAANG and even among people carrying "senior" titles at these places, have little experience with "software design principles" -- tens of thousands of brilliant Ivy League graduates with surreal compensation packages have spent the last decade pulling tickets off JIRA and pasting least-change-possible patches onto existing code for about 10 hours a week while spending the other 30+ hours barely engaged at meetings. reply WesleyJohnson 5 days ago | root | parent | next [–] This is maddening. To think I could've memorized some leet code problems, got a job at FAANG and been making 300k base for the past 5+ years while working 10-hour weeks is - yep, maddening. reply taurath 4 days ago | root | parent | next [–] The best time to be aware of the socioeconomic class differences in tech was 20 years ago, the second best time is now.
